turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Morning, Ray. Before you go in, blood pressure was one hundred and forty-six over eighty-eight, pulse seventy-six, temperature thirty-six point seven.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): One forty-six? I don't know, nurse. The chemist said something lower last time, but I can't remember the figure.
[SEG0003] person_3 (CAREGIVER): He always thinks the chemist machine was kinder. I'd go with today's.
[SEG0004] person_1 (NURSE): On the repeat list I've got ibuprofen four hundred milligrams three times a day, and a water tablet each morning. Is that what you actually take?
[SEG0005] person_2 (PATIENT): The water tablet, yeah, little white one, but I don't know the name of it. The ibuprofen, no, I buy the Nurofen two hundreds for my back. I don't take four hundred.
[SEG0006] person_3 (CAREGIVER): The box at home is the four hundred milligram ones the GP gave him. He takes a two hundred when he thinks of it, that's the thing.
[SEG0007] person_4 (DOCTOR): Thanks, I'll untangle that in a minute. Come on through, Ray. What are we dealing with?
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): My back. The bottom of it. Really sore.
[SEG0009] person_4 (DOCTOR): How long has it been like that?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): I don't know, doctor. A few weeks? Or since the move. I can't separate the two.
[SEG0011] person_3 (CAREGIVER): We moved six weeks ago Saturday. He was hauling boxes that first weekend and he's grumbled ever since, so it's six weeks, not a few.
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): It wasn't from day one. I'd say three weeks, honestly. Maybe. I don't know.
[SEG0013] person_4 (DOCTOR): Alright. So between you I'm hearing roughly three weeks to about six weeks, and neither of you is nailing it. We'll park it as that range.
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah. Sorry. The move was chaos, boxes everywhere, the kettle still isn't—
[SEG0015] person_3 (CAREGIVER): She doesn't need the kettle.
[SEG0016] person_4 (DOCTOR): Whereabouts is the pain, and how bad, out of ten?

[SEG0017] person_2 (PATIENT): Across the bottom, just above the belt. Whatever the exact number of weeks is. Most days a three or four out of ten, and if I lift it's more like a seven. Sharp when it grabs.
[SEG0018] person_3 (CAREGIVER): He couldn't get his socks on yesterday, that's how bad—
[SEG0019] person_2 (PATIENT): I did get them on. It just took forever.
[SEG0020] person_4 (DOCTOR): Does it travel down the leg?
[SEG0021] person_2 (PATIENT): Not really down the leg. Stays in the back. Though if I sit in the van too long...
[SEG0022] person_4 (DOCTOR): The van?
[SEG0023] person_2 (PATIENT): Driving between the sites, yeah. Then the left foot goes all tingly. Pins and needles. Not pain exactly, just odd.
[SEG0024] person_4 (DOCTOR): Any proper numbness in that foot, or round the groin, the saddle area?
[SEG0025] person_2 (PATIENT): The foot isn't numb, it's that tingle. The groin, when we shifted the sofa I caught it on the—
[SEG0026] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Feeling, Ray. She's asking about feeling.
[SEG0027] person_2 (PATIENT): Sorry. No. No numbness down there. I'm sure of that. I don't know about the medical words.
[SEG0028] person_4 (DOCTOR): Any trouble passing water, leaking, not getting there in time?
[SEG0029] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Loo's been normal.
[SEG0030] person_4 (DOCTOR): And the bowels, any loss of control?
[SEG0031] person_3 (CAREGIVER): He'd have told me. He tells me everything else, including the neighbour's—
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): No, bowels are fine. Bit constipated since the co-codamol, but I stopped that.
[SEG0033] person_4 (DOCTOR): We'll come back to the co-codamol. Any fever, or waking up drenched?
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): No fever. I stuck a thermometer in a couple of nights because Sandra fussed. It was normal. No sweats either, now you say it.
[SEG0035] person_4 (DOCTOR): Have you lost weight?
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): I don't think so. I don't know, doctor. I've been skipping lunch, that's all.
[SEG0037] person_3 (CAREGIVER): His work trousers are hanging off him. Half a stone, easy, since the move.
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): I haven't lost weight. Those trousers were always big. I don't own scales.
[SEG0039] person_4 (DOCTOR): So you say no weight loss, Sandra says about half a stone, and we can't check it today. Does the pain wake you at night?
[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): It aches after a heavy shift, but it doesn't wake me up screaming. Lying flat actually eases it.
[SEG0041] person_4 (DOCTOR): What sets it off in the daytime?
[SEG0042] person_2 (PATIENT): Lifting at the warehouse. I'm a picker, totes all day. Sitting in that van. Bending for the bottom shelf.
[SEG0043] person_4 (DOCTOR): And what settles it, apart from lying flat?
[SEG0044] person_2 (PATIENT): The Nurofen, a bit. Heat pack. Walking's better than standing still, which is weird.
[SEG0045] person_3 (CAREGIVER): If he takes the tablets. Some days the strip hasn't been touched.
[SEG0046] person_2 (PATIENT): I take them when it's bad. I don't know if that's every day. Not three times, anyway.

[SEG0047] person_4 (DOCTOR): Let me say it back. Nurofen, which is ibuprofen, is on the list as four hundred milligrams three times a day. You think you buy the two hundred milligram ones for the back, Sandra says the box at home is four hundred, and you use them as and when. Is that fair?
[SEG0048] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah, that's fair. I don't know the dose for certain, if I'm honest.
[SEG0049] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I'll bring the box next time. Should've shoved it in my bag. I brought the wrong bag, the one with the shopping list and—
[SEG0050] person_4 (DOCTOR): The box will help. And the water tablet, the little white one in the morning, you still can't name it?
[SEG0051] person_2 (PATIENT): No. It's for my blood pressure. Been on it for years. I just swallow it with the tea.
[SEG0052] person_4 (DOCTOR): High blood pressure is on your record, and it's ongoing. Anything else? Diabetes, cancer, osteoporosis?
[SEG0053] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Just the blood pressure. My dad had a rotten back and ended up having an operation, but that's him.
[SEG0054] person_4 (DOCTOR): Any operations on you?
[SEG0055] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Never been put under.
[SEG0056] person_4 (DOCTOR): Allergies to medicines?
[SEG0057] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Nothing I'm allergic to.
[SEG0058] person_3 (CAREGIVER): That's not what you told them at the dental hospital. Penicillin. A rash, when they took that tooth out.
[SEG0059] person_2 (PATIENT): I don't remember a rash. I don't know, doctor. I don't think I'm allergic to it.
[SEG0060] person_4 (DOCTOR): I'll mark penicillin as disputed, not confirmed, until someone finds the letter. You mentioned co-codamol.
[SEG0061] person_2 (PATIENT): The chemist sold me co-codamol. I think it was the thirty slash five hundred ones. Made me queasy, so I stopped after two days.
[SEG0062] person_4 (DOCTOR): And plain paracetamol?
[SEG0063] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah. Two tablets, by mouth, when the Nurofen isn't enough. Not every day.
[SEG0064] person_4 (DOCTOR): Do you smoke?
[SEG0065] person_2 (PATIENT): Packed it in. Ten years back. I was on about twenty a day before that.
[SEG0066] person_4 (DOCTOR): And drink?
[SEG0067] person_2 (PATIENT): A couple of pints on a Friday. That's me done.
[SEG0068] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Three or four if United are on. Not in the week, though.
[SEG0069] person_2 (PATIENT): Alright, some Fridays it's more. I don't know exactly. Depends if the pub's showing it.
[SEG0070] person_4 (DOCTOR): Who's at home with you?
[SEG0071] person_2 (PATIENT): Just me, since the move. Sandra's a paid carer, four mornings a week, does the heavy bits I can't.
[SEG0072] person_4 (DOCTOR): Right. I'll examine you. Can you stand for me?
[SEG0073] person_2 (PATIENT): Yep. Give me a second. The floor's a long way down today.

[SEG0074] person_4 (DOCTOR): Tender over the lower lumbar muscles, both sides, a bit more on the left. No bony tenderness in the midline that worries me. Straight leg raise is clear both sides, no pain shooting down.
[SEG0075] person_4 (DOCTOR): Power at the knees and ankles is normal. I can't find a definite numb patch on the left foot, despite the tingling you describe. The pulses in both feet are fine.
[SEG0076] person_2 (PATIENT): The tingle isn't there this minute, to be fair. Comes on in the van.
[SEG0077] person_4 (DOCTOR): Putting it together, this behaves like mechanical low back pain, from the lifting round the move and the warehouse work. I'm not calling it a slipped disc today.

[SEG0078] person_4 (DOCTOR): The foot tingling means I can't completely rule out some nerve irritation, but there's no red flag for cauda equina. No fever, and the bladder and saddle feeling are alright.
[SEG0079] person_2 (PATIENT): So no scan, then?
[SEG0080] person_4 (DOCTOR): Not today. If it hasn't settled when I see you, we might arrange an MRI of the lumbar spine. I'm not booking that now.

[SEG0081] person_4 (DOCTOR): I'll see you back in two weeks. Keep moving, little walks, no heavy totes if you can swap the duties, and use the paracetamol, two tablets up to four times a day, rather than waiting till you're floored.
[SEG0082] person_2 (PATIENT): What about the Nurofen?

[SEG0083] person_4 (DOCTOR): Until we know the strength, don't increase it. Bring the box. If you suddenly can't pass urine, or the saddle area goes numb, or the pain turns savage with weakness, that's A&E the same day, not a wait for me.
[SEG0084] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I'll bring the box, and I'll stop him pretending he knows the dose. Reception on the way out, yeah?

spec.situation: Manual worker or office worker with low back pain for 'a few weeks or since the move'; doctor asks about red flags (numbness, bladder, weight loss, fever) one by one; patient answers some clearly, some vaguely or with a story. Painkiller use mentioned.
features: disputed_numbers: the nurse reads a value and the patient or relative disagrees or remembers another (a dose, a weight, a BP). Keep both and record an uncertainty.
hedged_plan: the doctor hedges ('we might do a scan if it does not settle', 'let's see in two weeks'). Conditional vs planned status must follow the words.
interruptions_trailing_off: people interrupt each other, trail off, or the answer comes two turns after the question.

colloquial_drug_names: medicines referred to by colour, purpose or brand ('the water tablet', 'Crocin', 'my sugar tablets', 'the purple inhaler'); the name is recorded as said, the normalized name only if it is clear.
